edition.deck: Security warnings, a fragile Ukraine truce and fresh political disputes lead the day’s coverage, alongside stories on Britain’s wildlife and Denmark’s infrastructure.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise developments with clear public consequence. Treat claims about political motives, attacks and unresolved investigations with care; several continuing stories have appeared in earlier editions, so include them only where the gather offers a meaningful new development.

content.headline: Zelenskyy says Ukraine received no warning before Russian missile strike
content.shortHeadline: Zelenskyy says allies gave no warning before Kyiv missile strike
content.standfirst: Ukraine’s president says five missiles hit civilian infrastructure in Kyiv without advance warning from partners. He also says Russian attacks have continued despite Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire.

image.caption: Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv.

sources.originalTitle: Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy
Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
Trump is always sowing chaos. Europe just needs to hold its nerve

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine received no early warning from its partners before a Russian ballistic missile strike hit civilian infrastructure in Kyiv on Monday. He called the attack “particularly vile” and said advance intelligence about ballistic missiles helps save lives. Ukraine’s foreign minister said the lack of warning was due to a “special type” of Russian weapon.

segments.title: Truce claims and support
segments.body: Zelenskyy says Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite Trump’s claim that the two sides agreed to an energy ceasefire. The Kremlin has not confirmed it agreed to the arrangement. The Guardian reports that Washington has threatened to suspend intelligence sharing and weapons support if Kyiv does not stop attacks on Russian energy sites.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s analysis argues that Europe has more capacity to support Ukraine independently than it did earlier in the war, and should not let each shift in Trump’s position prompt panic.

content.headline: Bulgaria summons Russian envoy after drone strikes hit two Black Sea ships
content.shortHeadline: Bulgaria summons Russian envoy after Black Sea ship strikes
content.standfirst: One merchant ship sank and 10 crew members are missing after drone strikes off Bulgaria. Sofia says there is no conclusive evidence of responsibility, while its defence minister said Russia was the likeliest culprit.

image.caption: The Ukrainian-owned cargo ship Chelsea-3 was struck by drones off Bulgaria; its crew were rescued.

sources.originalTitle: Bulgaria summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack

segments.body: Two merchant ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. The Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity sank, with six crew rescued and 10 missing; all 15 people aboard the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea-3 were rescued. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned Russia’s ambassador after the attacks.

segments.title: Responsibility remains disputed
segments.body: Radev said there was no conclusive evidence against either side, though he said the outcome appeared to benefit Russia. Bulgaria’s defence minister said officials assumed the drones were Russian, while the Russian ambassador said she had no information from Moscow’s defence ministry and suggested a third party could be responsible. Russia has not publicly commented.

content.headline: US agents search Ilhan Omar’s home in an unspecified federal investigation
content.shortHeadline: US agents search Ilhan Omar’s home; investigation remains unclear
content.standfirst: Federal agents carried out a court-authorised search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home, but the Justice Department has not said what the investigation concerns. Omar calls it political intimidation; Trump denies involvement.

image.caption: Federal agents outside Representative Ilhan Omar’s home.

sources.originalTitle: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
DR-korrespondent om ransagning af Trump-kritiker: Timingen er 'mystisk'

segments.body: Homeland Security Investigations agents searched the Washington-area home of Representative Ilhan Omar under a judicially authorised warrant, the Justice Department says. It has described the matter only as an ongoing federal criminal investigation. Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of Donald Trump, said the search was an attempt to target political opponents. Trump said he had nothing to do with the inquiry.

perspectives.body: DR’s US correspondent noted the timing, three weeks before the midterm elections, and said it was unusual for prosecutors to take steps involving candidates close to an election. He also stressed that he could not establish political motivation; Justice Department guidance bars action intended to influence an election, not investigations as such.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: Authorities have not confirmed what the investigation covers or whether earlier allegations about Omar’s immigration records are part of it. Omar has denied wrongdoing. The search took place as she campaigns for re-election on 3 November.

content.headline: Brazil court scandal adds pressure to Lula ahead of presidential runoff
content.shortHeadline: Brazil court scandal threatens Lula’s re-election bid
content.standfirst: A dispute over alleged links between Supreme Court justices and a banker accused of fraud has damaged confidence in the court, the Guardian reports. Analysts say the crisis may have helped Jair Bolsonaro’s son gain ground ahead of the 25 October runoff.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro, who is running against incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential runoff.

sources.originalTitle: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

segments.body: Brazil’s Supreme Court is at the centre of a political crisis just days before the 25 October presidential runoff. The Guardian reports that a police investigation found a contract worth about £20m between a bank accused of fraud and a law firm run by Justice Alexandre de Moraes’s wife. Moraes denies wrongdoing and disputes the authenticity of messages said to link him to the banker.

segments.title: Political consequences
segments.body: Analysts cited by the Guardian say the scandal has weakened confidence in the court and may have contributed to Flávio Bolsonaro’s rise ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The report also says investigations have found links between the banker and other justices; those implicated deny wrongdoing. The election’s outcome remains uncertain.

content.headline: Taliban suspend BBC FM broadcasts across Afghanistan
content.shortHeadline: Taliban suspend BBC FM broadcasts in Afghanistan
content.standfirst: The Taliban government says it has suspended BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites over unspecified “repeated violations”. The BBC says its services remain available by other means, including shortwave and online.

sources.originalTitle: BBC FM radio transmissions suspended in Afghanistan

segments.body: Afghanistan’s Taliban government has suspended BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites nationwide, saying the decision followed “repeated violations” but giving no details. The BBC says it is working with the authorities and continues to broadcast in Pashto, Dari and English by shortwave and medium wave, as well as online and by satellite.

segments.title: Reach beyond FM
segments.body: The BBC says its services reach more than a fifth of Afghanistan’s adult population each week and include educational programmes aimed at girls, who are barred from secondary school. Electricity shortages, cost and low literacy can limit access to alternatives, the report says.

content.headline: Indian opposition leaders detained at Delhi protest site
content.shortHeadline: Indian opposition leaders detained at Delhi protest site
content.standfirst: Leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party were detained after entering Jantar Mantar, where they were demanding the election chief resign over revised voter lists. Critics say the changes risk excluding eligible voters; the Election Commission rejects claims of bias.

image.caption: Cockroach Janta Party members enter Jantar Mantar before being detained.

sources.originalTitle: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site

segments.body: Police detained Cockroach Janta Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das after they climbed over barricades into Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi protest site. They were calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign over a revision of electoral rolls. It was not immediately clear where police took them.

segments.title: Dispute over voter lists
segments.body: Opposition parties say the revision risks removing eligible voters from the rolls; the Election Commission and the governing party reject accusations of bias. The federal government had removed Jantar Mantar’s status as a designated protest venue a day before the detentions. Congress has challenged the voter revision in the Supreme Court.

content.headline: Mexican officials released after gang kidnaps them to demand suspect’s release
content.shortHeadline: Mexican gang releases three officials after hostage deal
content.standfirst: A gang seized three employees of a prosecutor’s office after a senior member was arrested. Officials released the suspect to protect their staff; all three hostages were later freed, with one treated for a gunshot wound.

sources.originalTitle: Mexican gang kidnaps officials to force detained member's release

segments.body: Pueblos Unidos seized three employees of the attorney-general’s office in Mexico’s Morelos state after authorities arrested a senior gang member. The office says it released the detained suspect to safeguard its staff, and the gang later freed all three employees. One hostage was taken to hospital with a gunshot wound and was reported to be stable.

segments.title: A recurring tactic
segments.body: The office says the release followed official guidance to put the lives of hostages first, but said the kidnappings would not go unpunished. The BBC reports that Mexican criminal gangs have used violence to pressure authorities after arrests of senior figures, including in earlier cases involving the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

content.headline: MI5 chief warns of rising state threats, AI risks and extremist violence
content.shortHeadline: MI5 chief warns of rising state threats and AI risks
content.standfirst: Ken McCallum says threats from foreign adversaries have quadrupled in a decade and warns that terrorists are exploring the use of AI. He also describes a rise in far-right cases and confirms Russian attempts to influence the Brexit referendum.

image.caption: MI5 director general Ken McCallum delivers his annual speech at Thames House in London.

sources.originalTitle: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief says
UK at growing risk of terror attack with deadly man-made viruses, warns MI5 boss
MI5-chef advarer om intensiverede iranske angreb
Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms

segments.body: MI5 director general Ken McCallum says the service is devoting more resources to countering state threats than at any point during the Cold War. He named Russia as the leading state threat and said Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the UK in the past year. Iran’s role in the RAF Fairford incident remains an allegation; seven people have been arrested and bailed.

segments.title: Terrorism and AI
segments.body: McCallum said the most marked recent trend in MI5’s caseload was people moving from extremist anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievances towards terrorist intent. He cited an investigation into a radicalised 13-year-old. MI5 has also launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre; McCallum warned that extremist groups could use AI to develop bioweapons, a risk he said has not yet materialised.

segments.title: What MI5 said about Brexit
segments.body: McCallum confirmed that Russian media and online accounts tried to influence the 2016 referendum, but said there was a distinction between attempted interference and an effect on the result. He warned that prolonged debate could exaggerate the impact of Russian activity. The referendum result, he said, was not in dispute.

content.headline: Reform leaders row over whether troops could use lethal force against small-boat
content.shortHeadline: Reform leaders clash over lethal force against small boats
content.standfirst: Nigel Farage says a Reform government would not authorise routine lethal force against people crossing the Channel, after Robert Jenrick said the Royal Marines should be able to fire if necessary. The dispute exposes divisions over the party’s policy.

image.caption: Robert Jenrick said the Royal Marines should be able to use lethal force against small boats if necessary.

sources.originalTitle: Farage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claim

segments.body: Nigel Farage has rejected the idea that a Reform UK government would authorise routine lethal force against people crossing the Channel in small boats. The statement followed Reform MP Robert Jenrick’s comments that the Royal Marines should be deployed to return boats to France and allowed to use lethal force if necessary. Farage said force would be justified only if troops were fired on.

segments.title: Political and legal objections
segments.body: Reform chair Zia Yusuf also said force would be limited to circumstances where it was necessary to protect life. Defence minister Luke Pollard called the proposal “disgusting and illegal”, saying the armed forces must not accept an unlawful order. The Guardian reports that the row came amid signs of internal tensions and a poll showing Reform in third place.

content.headline: UK wild bird populations fall to their lowest level on record
content.shortHeadline: UK wild bird populations hit record low, with 45% declining
content.standfirst: Average populations of 132 native breeding species fell by 19% between 1970 and 2025, figures compiled for the government show. Farmland birds and seabirds have suffered particularly steep declines, though some conservation efforts have produced gains.

image.caption: A skylark, one of the farmland birds whose population has declined.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on record

segments.body: Wild bird populations in the UK have fallen to their lowest level since records began, according to figures from conservation bodies. Average populations across 132 native breeding species dropped by 19% between 1970 and 2025. Nearly half of monitored species declined over the past five years, with 55% falling in England.

segments.title: Farmland and seabirds hardest hit
segments.body: Farmland bird populations are down 63% since 1970, while seabirds have fallen by more than a fifth in five years. Conservationists cite farming changes and avian flu among the pressures. Some species have increased, including red kites and cranes; experts say that shows recovery is possible with sustained conservation work.

content.headline: Falklands dispute intensifies as UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s arrest
content.shortHeadline: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s Falklands oil arrest requests
content.standfirst: Britain says Argentina’s requests to arrest people linked to a Falklands oil project are politically motivated. The Guardian reports that Buenos Aires may also seek international arbitration over the project, but neither legal move has yet produced a ruling.

image.caption: A road on the Falkland Islands between Mount Pleasant and Stanley.

sources.originalTitle: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests

segments.body: The UK has asked Interpol to reject Argentine requests for “red notices” seeking the arrest of people involved in the Sea Lion oil project off the Falkland Islands. British officials argue the requests are politically motivated. Interpol says it will follow its constitution, which bars it from political intervention; member countries decide whether to act on notices.

segments.title: A wider sovereignty dispute
segments.body: Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block the project, which the Falklands government says could substantially increase the islands’ economy. The Guardian reports that Argentina is expected to seek arbitration under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. UK officials argue that the dispute concerns sovereignty, which the tribunal is unlikely to address.

content.headline: Bellway says first-time buyer scheme could lift annual housebuilding by 10%
content.shortHeadline: Bellway says buyer scheme could boost housebuilding by 10%
content.standfirst: The housebuilder says Andy Burnham’s proposed Your First Home programme could help lift its annual completions to 10,000, though some buyers may delay purchases until details are confirmed. The scheme’s terms and launch date are still to come.

image.caption: Bellway is targeting 9,000 to 9,400 home completions in the current year.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’

segments.body: Bellway chief executive Jason Honeyman says the government’s proposed Your First Home scheme could increase the builder’s annual output by about 10%. The programme would offer first-time buyers in England a government-backed equity loan of 20% of a new-build purchase price, with a minimum deposit of 2.5%. Full details are expected in the 28 October Budget.

segments.title: A potential boost, with a near-term risk
segments.body: Honeyman said the scheme could help Bellway return to at least 10,000 completions a year from next September at the earliest, but warned it might slow the market in the short term as buyers wait for its launch. The company is currently targeting 9,000 to 9,400 homes this year, amid weaker demand and higher construction costs.

content.headline: Government review warns ADHD and autism diagnoses could risk overdiagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Review warns ADHD diagnoses may risk overdiagnosis
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned report says diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism in some groups are approaching or exceeding estimated prevalence. The authors warn that this does not establish widespread overdiagnosis, but say the balance of risks may be changing.

image.caption: Reported ADHD and autism diagnoses have risen over the past decade.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: A government-commissioned review says NHS diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism among young people are approaching or, for some groups, exceeding estimates of how common the conditions are. ADHD diagnoses among teenage boys rose from 2% to 5% in a decade; among teenage girls, they rose from 0.5% to 2.5%.

segments.title: The report’s caution
segments.body: The review says the figures do not, by themselves, prove that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale. It identifies several possible drivers of rising diagnoses, including changing definitions and awareness, and calls for better regulation of private assessment clinics. Experts differ on whether the present trend amounts to overdiagnosis or reflects unmet need.

content.headline: Fehmarn tunnel contractor reports cyber incident; details remain unknown
content.shortHeadline: Cyber incident reported at Fehmarn tunnel project
content.standfirst: FLC, the contractor building the Fehmarn Belt link, has told project owner Sund & Bælt it experienced a cyber incident. Neither company has said what happened or whether construction or other operations were affected.

image.caption: Construction work on the Fehmarn Belt tunnel project near Rødbyhavn.

sources.originalTitle: Femern-byggeri ramt af 'cyberhændelse'

segments.body: FLC, the contractor on the Fehmarn Belt tunnel project, has reported a “cyber incident” to project owner Sund & Bælt. The owner says it is in contact with FLC but has no further information. It remains unclear what the incident involved or whether it disrupted work on the project.

segments.title: Impact not confirmed
segments.body: A Danish Business Confederation cybersecurity adviser said incidents can become operational problems that prevent a company from carrying out core work, but the organisation has no specific information about the Fehmarn incident. No details have been released on its cause or consequences.

content.headline: Danish insurer reports 69% rise in cocaine treatment cases among employees
content.shortHeadline: Danica reports 69% rise in workplace cocaine treatment cases
content.standfirst: Danica says the number of cocaine-related treatment cases among employees at its corporate clients rose 69% from 2019 to 2025. An addiction counsellor points to easy access and workplace pressure, while a business association says employers should address the issue openly.

image.caption: Graphic showing Danica’s reported rise in cocaine-misuse treatment cases among corporate clients.

sources.originalTitle: Pensionsselskab oplever voldsom stigning: Kokain rammer danske arbejdspladser

segments.body: Pension company Danica says cocaine-related treatment cases among employees at its corporate clients increased by 69% between 2019 and 2025. Over the same period, its alcohol-misuse treatment cases fell by 10%. Danica says more businesses are asking how to prevent and respond to substance misuse among staff.

segments.title: Workplace response
segments.body: Addiction counsellor Anne-Margrethe Overgaard says cocaine has become easier to obtain and cheaper, and links its use by some workers to pressure to perform. An employers’ association representing machinery contractors says it has found value in discussing drugs openly, but does not believe the problem is greater in its own industries.

content.headline: Teachers describe dozens of special arrangements for pupils in Danish schools
content.shortHeadline: Teachers say pupil support arrangements are overwhelming classes
content.standfirst: Two teachers describe managing dozens of individual arrangements for pupils, from extra breaks to changes in arrival times. One says the growing workload reflects a public school system struggling to provide full inclusion.

image.caption: Teacher Signe Kløve Dreyer holds a list of individual arrangements for pupils.

sources.originalTitle: Nu står flere lærere frem: Signe skal huske 38 ønsker om særbehandling til elever

segments.body: Teacher Signe Kløve Dreyer says she has managed 38 individual arrangements for pupils in recent years. At Ulfborg School, teacher Gitte Bach says she has agreements in 23 of her class’s 29 weekly lessons, including adjusted arrival times and breaks. Both describe the practical burden of keeping track of different needs.

segments.title: The strain on class time
segments.body: Dreyer says the number of arrangements reflects a school system not equipped for full inclusion, and that time spent supporting individual pupils can leave less attention for the rest of the class. Bach says she is willing to make arrangements that help a pupil stay in school, but believes their volume has become too great.

content.headline: Fyn municipalities tighten rules on backyard poultry after noise complaints
content.shortHeadline: Fyn municipalities tighten rules on backyard poultry
content.standfirst: Nyborg now bars roosters where the nearest neighbour is less than 100 metres away, after the municipality says it receives about 20 complaints a year. A long-time breeder says the rules could undermine his breeding work and club.

image.caption: Jørgen Hansen stands outside the chicken run he has kept for more than 50 years.

sources.originalTitle: Efter 50 år må Jørgen ikke længere have galende haner: 'Det er tåbeligt'

segments.body: Several municipalities on Funen have tightened rules on keeping poultry in back gardens after complaints about noise. In Nyborg, residents may not keep roosters if a neighbour lives within 100 metres. The municipality says it receives about 20 complaints about the issue each year.

segments.title: Breeders object
segments.body: Jørgen Hansen, who has bred chickens for more than 50 years, says he cannot continue breeding without roosters and fears the rules could threaten his club. His neighbour says the birds cause no disturbance. Odense has also recently introduced new rules.

content.headline: Aalborg’s old crematorium cannot fit some coffins; replacement due in 2032
content.shortHeadline: Aalborg coffins travel hundreds of kilometres for cremation
content.standfirst: Some coffins are too wide for Aalborg’s ageing crematorium, so families may face longer waits and extra transport to facilities in Kolding or Aabenraa. The municipality has set aside DKK 158m for a replacement expected to open in 2032.

sources.originalTitle: Afdøde må køres tværs gennem landet for at blive brændt: Ovnene er for smalle

segments.body: Aalborg’s crematorium, built in 1969, is often out of service and its ovens cannot take some wider coffins. As a result, some deceased people must be transported hundreds of kilometres to Kolding or Aabenraa for cremation, increasing costs for families and potentially delaying the return of ashes.

segments.title: A six-year wait
segments.body: The municipality has allocated DKK 158m for a new crematorium, expected to be ready in 2032. It will have three ovens, including one designed for larger coffins, and room for a fourth. A city councillor says the existing ovens may last only until 2030 or 2031, but says the new building, equipment and fuel choices will take time.

content.headline: Fontaines D.C. turn modern unease into a darkly seductive triumph
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C. turn unease into a seductive triumph
content.standfirst: On their fifth album, the Dublin band transform anxieties about identity and online life into richly melodic, often overwhelming songs. The Guardian hears a group newly confident in its expansive sound.

image.caption: Fontaines D.C.

sources.originalTitle: Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph

segments.body: Dopamine Chamber takes on social media’s collapse of context and the erosion of truth, but its lyrics do not simply echo the news. Grian Chatten’s words promise escape even as they leave doubt about what that escape might cost. The Guardian finds the band’s dark, alluring arrangements make that tension hard to resist.

segments.title: A band growing into its scale
segments.body: After the arena-sized ambitions of Romance, the group’s latest record sounds more cohesive and assured. The review singles out the Rosalía duet “Where Is Gone?” as a highlight, and argues that the band’s ability to combine grand gestures with fine detail gives the album its force.

content.headline: Sophia Stel turns imposter syndrome into a boldly titled debut album
content.shortHeadline: Sophia Stel’s bold debut challenges imposter syndrome
content.standfirst: The Vancouver artist’s self-produced pop draws on a meteoric year, financial uncertainty and an unconventional upbringing. She explains why the album title The Greatest Album of All Time is only partly a joke.

image.caption: Sophia Stel

sources.originalTitle: ‘Girls aren’t supposed to be cocky’: Sophia Stel on the pressure of writing The Greatest Album Of All Time

segments.body: Sophia Stel’s debut follows the rapid rise of “I’ll Take It” on TikTok, two EPs and a deal with A24’s record label. Yet she has continued to take painting and bartending jobs while establishing herself as a musician, and says she is still learning to manage the pressure and imposter syndrome that have come with that change.

segments.title: Confidence, on her own terms
segments.body: The album title grew from a joke about wanting to make the greatest record ever, but Stel has kept its brashness. She says girls are not always encouraged to be cocky and that she is trying to give herself a louder voice. Growing up in a large, ultra-religious family also left her wary when others insist that things must be a certain way.

content.headline: The Go-Betweens’ reissues revisit a brilliant, turbulent band story
content.shortHeadline: The Go-Betweens: brilliant songs, turbulent history
content.standfirst: A new run of reissues brings the Australian group’s music back into view. The i Paper traces how Robert Forster, Grant McLennan and their collaborators made literary pop amid personal upheaval—and why the band’s legacy needs to include its women.

image.caption: Grant McLennan and Robert Forster of the Go-Betweens in 2000.

sources.originalTitle: The messy, bizarre inside story of The Go-Betweens

segments.body: The Go-Betweens built intricate pop songs around contrasting songwriting voices: Robert Forster’s sardonic, oblique writing and Grant McLennan’s more direct melodic gifts. Their new releases include the 1987 live album Fountains of Youth and reissues of several studio records.

segments.title: The people inside the songs
segments.body: The band’s relationships shaped its music and contributed to the collapse of its classic line-up after 16 Lovers Lane. The article also challenges accounts that have sidelined drummer Lindy Morrison and multi-instrumentalist Amanda Brown, noting Brown’s view that the women felt erased from the band’s history.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s last album is an unexpected farewell
content.standfirst: Marc Almond and Dave Ball had finished Danceteria together just two days before Ball died in 2025. Almond reflects on their long partnership and the New York nightlife that inspired the duo’s final record.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Danceteria is Soft Cell’s sixth and final album. Almond says he would not make another record under the band’s name without Ball, his musical partner for almost 50 years. The pair agreed the new songs were finished shortly before Ball’s death, aged 66.

segments.title: A portrait of New York after dark
segments.body: The album looks back to the pair’s early-1980s experiences in New York clubs, where freedom and creative possibility existed alongside loneliness and, as the AIDS crisis grew, fear. Almond describes the record as a closing circle: he was relieved they made it together, but saddened Ball would not see its release.

content.headline: Jamie T looks back on panic, growing up and the cost of touring Europe
content.shortHeadline: Jamie T on anxiety and why Europe tours no longer add up
content.standfirst: As he releases Ghosts (100 Days of Morning), the singer-songwriter revisits the early years that shaped him and describes the financial barriers to taking his band back to Europe. He also discusses panic disorder and the challenge of outgrowing teenage songs.

image.caption: Jamie T

sources.originalTitle: Jamie T: ‘I can’t afford to tour Europe anymore’

segments.body: Jamie T says his new album looks back on the period when he began writing music as a teenager, in part to help him move on. He discusses living with panic disorder, which made early touring exhausting, and says he still experiences anxiety, though not as severely as before.

segments.title: The economics of the road
segments.body: Touring with a band has become too expensive for Jamie T to take the new record around Europe. He says the numbers have not worked since Brexit, despite his wish to keep the band employed and bring the album to audiences beyond the UK.

content.headline: Beth Orton’s latest songs make for an adventurous, emotionally charged show
content.shortHeadline: Beth Orton makes her recent work the heart of a live set
content.standfirst: Rather than rely on the songs that made her name, Orton built her Brighton concert around her last two albums. The Guardian describes an experimental performance that moves from abstraction to a battered kind of optimism.

image.caption: Beth Orton performing at Concorde 2 in Brighton.

sources.originalTitle: Beth Orton review – battered optimism from an artist making the best music of her career

segments.body: Orton’s set at Brighton’s Concorde 2 drew mainly on The Ground Above and Weather Alive, with only one older favourite among the songs described. A jazz-rooted band and Orton’s keyboard-led performance steered the music away from the familiar sound of her early records.

The review highlights arrangements that blur the line between voice and instrument, including a trumpet part that shifts from breathy colour to dense, effected noise. The songs dwell on sleeplessness, loss and time passing, but the closing “Otherside” gathers that unease into an anthemic, hard-won optimism.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall set turns new songs into future standards
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance becomes a live album
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo live record captures an evening that was already becoming part of his story. Pitchfork hears a set of expansive piano performances that recast difficult songs as controlled, compelling works.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Recorded at Carnegie Hall in December 2025, Winter’s solo performance is released as a live album alongside a concert film. The set includes three unreleased songs, and the review argues that stripping the material back to voice and piano lets its melodies and emotional shifts come into focus.

segments.title: A performance becoming a story
segments.body: The review hears Winter’s new songs as some of his strongest work, especially “If You Turn Back Now,” which moves from a breakup song into an apocalyptic, hymnlike climax. It also cautions that the recording and film capture not just a concert but the rapid construction of a young performer’s public mythology.

content.headline: Jess Williamson settles into her own sound on A Mile South of Heaven
content.shortHeadline: Jess Williamson finds her footing in country on a searching album
content.standfirst: On her sixth solo album, Williamson works through the pull between Texas and Los Angeles without trying to resolve it. Pitchfork praises the way her voice and writing turn that tension into intimate country songs.

sources.originalTitle: A Mile South of Heaven

segments.body: Produced by Shooter Jennings, A Mile South of Heaven marks a fuller embrace of country music after Williamson’s earlier indie-rock influences. Pitchfork finds her more at ease in the style, while her songs keep returning to the emotional and geographical distance between home and the city.

The review singles out Williamson’s phrasing and the detail in her lyrics, where a place name or small shift in perspective can carry a larger history. Rather than romanticise constant escape, the album’s wandering narrator turns toward loneliness and family ties.

content.headline: Tom Rhys Harries takes on Clayface and its grotesque transformation
content.shortHeadline: Tom Rhys Harries takes the lead in DC horror Clayface
content.standfirst: After years of character roles, the Welsh actor leads a DC film that leans towards body horror rather than superhero spectacle. He talks about its gruesome make-up, his ADHD and the pressure of landing a major role.

image.caption: Tom Rhys Harries in rock ’n’ roll style.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain Clayface

segments.body: Harries plays Matt Hagen, an actor whose face is mutilated before an experimental serum restores his looks and gives him the power to change his appearance. The film’s horror includes a scene Harries calls its “tipping point of ickiness”, as the character cuts at his melting eyelids.

segments.title: A lead role and a different kind of comic-book film
segments.body: Harries says he felt ready for his first blockbuster lead after three months of auditions. He hopes Clayface can offer something different at a time when comic-book films are facing fatigue, though its commercial prospects remain uncertain.

content.headline: A rediscovered scrapbook reveals how F.W. Murnau made Faust
content.shortHeadline: A century-old scrapbook opens up Murnau’s Faust
content.standfirst: A production scrapbook assembled for the director after the shoot has resurfaced as a rare record of the making of Faust. Its sketches and photographs show how Murnau and his collaborators built the silent film’s striking images.

image.caption: Mephistopheles looms over a village in F.W. Murnau’s Faust.

sources.originalTitle: Devil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpiece

segments.body: The Faust Bible began as a prop used in F.W. Murnau’s film, then became a gift to the director: art directors Robert Herlth and Walter Röhrig filled its pages with designs, stills and behind-the-scenes photographs. Murnau left it in Berlin when he went to Hollywood; after an uncertain journey, it is now held by the Cinémathèque Française.

segments.title: Images built by a team
segments.body: The scrapbook pairs drawings with frames from the finished film, revealing how sets, lighting and camera movement worked together. Its diagrams also explain the low-tech illusion behind the sequence in which Mephistopheles flies Faust around the world.

content.headline: Critics disagree over whether The Social Reckoning can make its case
content.shortHeadline: Three critics find different limits in The Social Reckoning
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s drama follows a Facebook whistleblower and a journalist, but critics differ over its force. The Guardian sees a dated, constrained view of the internet; the i Paper finds it alarming, while BBC Culture says it lacks urgency.

image.caption: Jeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning isn’t as angry or as potent as a Facebook drama should be
I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises journalist Jeff Horwitz’s reporting on Facebook’s internal research and former employee Frances Haugen’s disclosures. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg, with Mikey Madison as Haugen and Jeremy Allen White as Horwitz. The Guardian argues that Sorkin’s film recognises social media’s real-world effects but frames them too narrowly.

segments.title: A warning with divided impact
segments.body: The i Paper found the story frightening, but says its force is blunted by how easily viewers can return to the platforms it criticises. BBC Culture also finds the film less urgent than its subject demands, while the Guardian criticises its limited view of the internet’s harms. Their verdicts differ, but all three question what the drama can change.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reviewer places the film’s warning against her own continued use of Meta products, arguing that repeated revelations can make audiences numb rather than spur them to act.

content.headline: Mag Mag turns infatuation and beauty norms into Japanese horror comedy
content.shortHeadline: Mag Mag makes a grotesque, playful turn in Japanese horror
content.standfirst: Yuriyan Retriever’s feature debut follows a towering ghost who pursues the men she loves. The Guardian finds a strange, fresh comedy-horror that also takes aim at bullying and ideas of feminine beauty.

image.caption: Sara Minami as Sanae and Oshiro Maeda as Hiroshi in Mag Mag.

sources.originalTitle: Mag Mag review – giant female ghost loves people to death in Japanese comedy-horror

segments.body: Mag Mag is a two-metre-tall ghost whose infatuation becomes lethal. The film unfolds in linked chapters, building a satirical horror story around obsession, bullying and beauty expectations. Sara Minami plays Sanae, a woman whose own fixation brings another strand of toxic desire into the story.

The review praises the film’s unruly tone and Minami’s comic performance, while noting a late twist that complicates its apparent account of who is victim and who is aggressor. Takashi Miike’s involvement is presented as a sign of a passing of the torch between generations of Japanese horror-makers.

content.headline: James Dean’s lasting appeal lies beyond the rebel image
content.shortHeadline: James Dean’s vulnerability survives the rebel mythology
content.standfirst: A new Netflix adaptation of East of Eden renews attention on Dean’s role as Cal. The i Paper revisits the actor’s short career and argues that his most affecting moments reveal a vulnerable young man, not just an icon of cool.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s first major film role, as Cal in Elia Kazan’s East of Eden, drew on his difficult relationship with his father. Kazan used that emotional history to shape Dean’s performance, including an unscripted moment when Cal reaches for an embrace from his father and is met with a rigid response.

segments.title: The person behind the image
segments.body: Dean died aged 24, after only three starring roles, and his early death helped fix his public image as a symbol of rebellion. The article argues that the fragile, needy Cal—rather than the familiar poster image of Dean in a leather jacket—is the performance that best explains his enduring hold on audiences.

content.headline: Forever Is Now follows an Irish politician in a favourable light
content.shortHeadline: Forever Is Now profiles former Irish Green leader Eamon Ryan
content.standfirst: The documentary follows Eamon Ryan’s final months in government and his decision to step down. The Guardian sees a principled, hard-working figure, but says the film leaves important political context unexplored.

image.caption: Eamon Ryan on the New York subway in Forever Is Now.

sources.originalTitle: Forever Is Now review – political study of former Irish Green leader is like The Thick of It but with morals

segments.body: Forever Is Now follows Ryan during his last 18 months as Ireland’s environment and transport minister, before he left government in 2025. Cameras accompany him through flood-hit communities, international climate meetings and the final days of his ministerial role.

segments.title: A portrait with gaps
segments.body: The film also shows Ryan with his autistic son, whose need for full-time care was one reason he gave for resigning. The Guardian notes that the documentary is a favourable portrait and says more explanation of Irish climate policy, the COP conferences and the Greens’ 2024 election defeat would have helped viewers understand the political stakes.

content.headline: Digger divides critics over Tom Cruise’s oversized eco-satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger splits critics over Cruise’s outlandish performance
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise plays an oil billionaire in Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s climate satire, a film that pushes his screen persona into unfamiliar territory. BBC Culture embraces the audacity; the i Paper argues that the performance overwhelms the character.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in prosthetic make-up in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: Digger casts Cruise as Digger Rockwell, an oil baron whose company’s actions trigger an environmental catastrophe. The film combines prosthetic transformation, political satire and an unusually self-aware performance, making its lead role a sharp departure from Cruise’s recent action-hero parts.

segments.title: Risk or overreach?
segments.body: The i Paper critic says Cruise’s careful self-consciousness makes it difficult to see the character, while BBC Culture considers the scale of his performance part of the film’s daredevil appeal. The reviews also differ on the film’s excess: both recognise its divisive ambition, but reach opposite conclusions about whether it works.

perspectives.body: BBC Culture sees Digger as a politically blunt, love-it-or-hate-it experiment whose eccentricity argues against treating it as a conventional awards play.

content.headline: Being Muslim After 9/11 asks what journalism chose to amplify
content.shortHeadline: Being Muslim After 9/11 questions journalism’s choices
content.standfirst: Mobeen Azhar’s documentary traces rising Islamophobia and hears from Muslim community leaders who challenge his earlier reporting. The Guardian praises his willingness to examine journalism’s own role in shaping public narratives.

image.caption: Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan in Being Muslim After 9/11.

sources.originalTitle: Being Muslim After 9/11 review – other journalists wouldn’t dare to air this

segments.body: Azhar looks back over 25 years since the 11 September attacks, exploring how life changed for British Muslims and how journalists covered the period. In the film, community figures Alyas Karmani and Farasat Latif argue that earlier reporting gave disproportionate attention to a radical fringe and helped reinforce Islamophobic narratives.

segments.title: Listening to criticism
segments.body: Azhar discusses those accusations with co-director Masood Khan, confronting a difficult question for journalists: how to report inconvenient truths without amplifying the people who exploit them. The film does not offer an easy answer, but the Guardian values its willingness to leave the disagreement and the consequences of past editorial choices in view.

content.headline: Tyson review: a troubling documentary gives its subject too much control
content.shortHeadline: Tyson is a troubling, insufficiently challenged portrait
content.standfirst: Netflix’s four-part series follows Mike Tyson from poverty to boxing fame, but the Guardian argues that its sympathetic framing fails to examine serious allegations with enough care. Donald Trump’s appearance deepens the unease.

image.caption: Mike Tyson in the Netflix docuseries Tyson.

sources.originalTitle: Tyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows up

segments.body: The series recounts Tyson’s rise from a difficult childhood to heavyweight champion, but also revisits his marriage to Robin Givens and his conviction for rape, which Tyson denies. The Guardian criticises the programme for giving his accounts room without applying comparable scrutiny to allegations and evidence.

segments.title: The cost of an authorised account
segments.body: The review describes the series as a sports biography with little distance from its subject, highlighting its use of interviews and archive footage around Givens and Tyson’s conviction. Trump’s defence of Tyson, and the documentary’s closing scene involving DMT, add to the critic’s concern about a production that seems more fascinated by its subject than accountable to the people affected by his actions.

content.headline: Carrie’s new adaptation divides critics over how much to change
content.shortHeadline: Carrie remake divides critics on its changes to the story
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s Prime Video series updates Stephen King’s novel, but critics disagree about its treatment of Carrie’s anger and agency. BBC Culture sees an effective modernisation; the i Paper says the reinvention weakens the story’s core.

image.caption: Summer H. Howell as Carrie.

sources.originalTitle: The Carrie remake made me furious
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: Both reviews focus on substantial changes to King’s story, including a Carrie who arrives at school after being home-schooled and a reworked account of her family. The i Paper critic argues that the series gives the heroine too little agency and shifts key moments to other characters. BBC Culture notes that the new setting brings social media into the story.

segments.title: Reinvention or loss?
segments.body: For the i Paper, softening Carrie’s anger undermines the revenge story that made the novel resonate. BBC Culture acknowledges that the adaptation departs from the book but considers it an engrossing coming-of-age horror with strong performances. The disagreement turns on whether the changes renew the story or dilute its central force.

perspectives.body: BBC Culture argues that Flanagan’s version works on its own terms: its present-day bullying and social-media pressures offer a new route into the familiar story.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a familiar legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up puts a British Asian family at its centre
content.standfirst: The BBC spin-off moves the divorce-law drama from London to Manchester, with a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its makers say the aim is both familiar relationship melodrama and everyday representation.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: Ritu Arya plays Aria Kishan, a barrister whose plans to take over her family’s law firm are disrupted by her mother’s death and her father’s changing intentions. Like The Split, the six-part series combines high-stakes divorce cases with conflicts inside the lawyers’ own family.

segments.title: Representation as ordinary life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary lives rather than being defined by a small set of familiar storylines. The series also puts women across writing, acting, casting and production roles, a priority for executive producer Abi Morgan.

content.headline: Richard Armitage on Winter, dark characters and his improvised pillow scene
content.shortHeadline: Richard Armitage on Winter and the appeal of dark roles
content.standfirst: The actor discusses his new ITV crime drama, his preference for intense characters and a scene in Netflix’s Obsession that was never meant to be sexy. He also reflects on privacy and the demands placed on public figures.

image.caption: Richard Armitage

sources.originalTitle: Winter’s Richard Armitage: ‘My pillow humping scene was improvised’

segments.body: Armitage plays forensic pathologist Ethan Winter, who works alongside DI Bell in a new case-of-the-week drama. He describes the character as deliberately provocative and says their relationship brings humour to the series. He also clarifies that the much-discussed pillow scene in Obsession was improvised to convey degradation, not eroticism.

segments.title: A private life, by choice
segments.body: Armitage says he is drawn to characters exploring grief, fear and violence, but keeps his own life separate from his work. He argues that performers have a right to privacy and worries that the expectation to make everything public can limit the audience’s ability to imagine them as characters.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week gives its familiar format a sharper edge
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off gets a welcome shake-up from audience-choice week
content.standfirst: Viewers set the challenges for the first audience-choice week, prompting unusual bakes and a less cosy mood in the tent. The i Paper sees a promising change to a format it says has grown too predictable.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: For the first time, viewers chose the challenges instead of judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. The bakers made individual technical challenges from basic ingredients and attempted wearable showstoppers, including a cake designed as a hat.

The article argues that the change brought a welcome dose of unpredictability to a show whose cosiness has started to feel stale. It also notes a livelier dynamic between Lawson and Hollywood, while cautioning that the series need not become cruel to keep its format fresh.

content.headline: Strictly’s early exit for Amy Dowden exposes the stakes of pairing
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden’s early Strictly exit raises questions about pairings
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that professional partners, not celebrity fame, are central to Strictly Come Dancing’s appeal. Amy Dowden’s second consecutive first-week exit prompts questions about how the show matches its dancers.

image.caption: Amy Dowden on Strictly Come Dancing.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: Dowden and celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton left the competition in week one, the second year running that her Strictly journey ended early. The article sets that result against her earlier difficult seasons, including an injury and treatment for breast cancer.

segments.title: The professional partners are the draw
segments.body: The critic argues that audiences invest in the professional dancers and the relationships they build with their partners, making the match-up a central part of the show’s appeal. Dowden, the article says, deserved a chance to be defined by her teaching and partnership rather than repeatedly by illness or an early exit.

content.headline: Treasure Island review: a reinvention leaves Jim Hawkins sidelined
content.shortHeadline: Treasure Island’s reinvention leaves Jim Hawkins adrift
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s review finds that a new six-part adaptation adds a power to Jim Hawkins but gives him little to do. David Oyelowo’s Long John Silver is a vivid exception in an otherwise derided reworking.

image.caption: Tom Sweet, David Oyelowo and Hayley Atwell in Treasure Island.

sources.originalTitle: Treasure Island review – this TV stinker does its best to ruin a literary classic

segments.body: The series gives Jim an unusually strong memory and makes his mother, Bess, more prominent in the pirate adventure. The Guardian argues that the changes do not make Jim more compelling, instead leaving the young hero watching as the adults take charge.

David Oyelowo brings force to Long John Silver, but the review criticises the dialogue, accents and added fantasy elements. It sees the series’ reimagining as a burden on the story rather than a fresh route into Stevenson’s novel.

content.headline: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse pairs vivid gothic design with punishing action
content.shortHeadline: Belmont’s Curse makes Castlevania more action-heavy
content.standfirst: The new Castlevania sends Rose Belmont through a demon-infested Paris and Dracula’s castle. The Guardian praises its frantic combat and gothic style, though its platforming and uneven exploration may frustrate series fans.

image.caption: Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.

sources.originalTitle: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled

segments.body: Belmont’s Curse shifts emphasis from role-playing and backtracking towards twitch-based combat and platforming challenges. Battles are fast and demanding, with enemies that punish missed dodges; the review says this focus may unsettle longtime fans but keeps the action lively.

The game’s strongest asset is its gothic Paris and castle, filled with striking details and imaginative encounters. The Guardian finds the quality uneven: some puzzles reward careful exploration, while other stretches rely on repetitive challenges and can drag.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has its best combat yet—and too little else
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day is let down by repetitive design
content.standfirst: The prequel revisits the first alien invasion, pairing spectacular combat with levels the Guardian finds repetitive and overstuffed. Its review sees a strong action system surrounded by too many familiar, frustrating routines.

image.caption: Marcus in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the series’ origin, following Marcus Fenix and his squad as the Locust emerge. The Guardian praises the combat as the best in the franchise, with weighty weapons, destructible environments and more fluid movement.

segments.title: The world keeps circling back
segments.body: The review criticises long stretches of repeated routes, oversized levels and collectibles that interrupt the story. It argues that the game’s strongest horror moments are too scarce to offset a campaign that shows its ideas early and then struggles to develop them.

content.headline: Resident Evil film recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil finds a new way to adapt the games
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger’s film leaves familiar heroes aside to follow an ordinary courier through a world of scarce ammunition, unsettling clues and escalating danger. The Guardian argues that this captures the games’ experience rather than just their characters.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger and actor Austin Abrams on the Resident Evil set.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich through an outbreak in Raccoon City, moving among locations familiar from the games while keeping him under-armed and unsure of what is happening. The article argues that the absence of series heroes such as Leon and Claire is deliberate: Cregger is adapting the tension and structure of play.

segments.title: Making the player part of the story
segments.body: Found recordings, brief exchanges with other characters and the search for scarce weapons echo how the games reveal their world. The feature places the film alongside other works that explore video-game rules and perspective, rather than simply translating a familiar plot.

content.headline: A gaming writer’s mobile-ad spiral exposes the grind of free-to-play ads
content.shortHeadline: Free mobile games turn one player into an ad-watching captive
content.standfirst: A short gaming break becomes a trail of low-cost mobile games, forced adverts and increasingly dubious promotions. The Guardian’s personal essay makes the irritation vivid while exposing the incentives built into free-to-play design.

image.caption: A screenshot from the Annoying Uncle Punch mobile game.

sources.originalTitle: Help! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming adverts

segments.body: The writer starts with a game that limits play unless users wait or watch adverts, then follows ads into a succession of mobile titles. Their promised hooks often fail to match the actual games, while attempts to skip or reject advertisements offer little relief.

segments.title: When the ads become the game
segments.body: As the session continues, promotions shift from games to gambling-style apps, cash-earning claims and health products. The essay uses the increasingly intrusive experience to show how free-to-play systems trade players’ time and attention for revenue.

content.headline: Roman fort in Pembrokeshire may connect a Welsh legend to real history
content.shortHeadline: Roman fort may link Welsh legend to real history
content.standfirst: Coins and other finds at a newly identified Roman site near Frenni Fawr give archaeologists evidence that a medieval story about Magnus Maximus may have a historical basis. They do not establish that the emperor was there.

image.caption: A mock-up of the Roman site in the Preseli Hills, Pembrokeshire.

sources.originalTitle: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real

segments.body: Archaeologists have identified a fortified Roman site in Pembrokeshire, about two miles south-west of Frenni Fawr. Two coins dated to the late fourth century, along with Roman tiles, pottery and compacted clay floors, support the identification of a military fort. The site is near the location named in the medieval Welsh tale The Dream of Macsen Wledig, about the emperor Magnus Maximus.

segments.title: What the finds can—and cannot—show
segments.body: The fort measures about 180 by 150 metres and may have housed around 500 troops, according to archaeologist Mark Merrony, who leads the excavation. Its buildings and layout are consistent with a military headquarters and a commander’s house. Merrony says the discoveries make the legend more compelling, but the finds do not prove that Magnus Maximus personally camped there.

content.headline: Study finds women with autoimmune conditions report more misdiagnoses
content.shortHeadline: Women report more autoimmune misdiagnoses
content.standfirst: A survey of more than 6,600 people with autoimmune conditions found women more often reported psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses and longer waits for diagnosis. The results describe patients’ experiences, not every clinical encounter.

sources.originalTitle: Women ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’

segments.body: In a study published in the Lancet eClinicalMedicine, 43% of women surveyed said they had been told their condition was psychiatric, compared with 33% of men. A third of women reported a psychosomatic misdiagnosis, compared with 22% of men. After adjustment for several factors, researchers found women were more likely than men to report both kinds of misdiagnosis.

segments.title: Diagnosis can take longer
segments.body: Women in the survey also reported more consultations and longer waits between symptoms and diagnosis: the most commonly reported wait for women was one to two years, while for men it was less than three months. The researchers note that autoimmune conditions can be difficult to diagnose because symptoms may be common to other illnesses. The study relied on patient reports, and most participants were women and from the UK.

content.headline: Optogenetic therapy improves vision for six of 10 patients in a trial
content.shortHeadline: Gene therapy improves vision for six patients
content.standfirst: A small study found meaningful improvement in six of 10 people treated for retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that damages light-sensitive cells in the eye. The approach is experimental and did not restore normal vision.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: The treatment uses gene therapy to make other cells in the retina respond to amber light, with patients wearing special glasses that convert ordinary light into amber. In a study published in The New England Journal of Medicine, six of 10 participants improved after three months. They could perform tasks such as picking up a cup, but could not distinguish between people’s faces.

segments.title: A wider research effort
segments.body: The technique, called optogenetics, uses light to activate nerve cells. Researchers are also investigating possible applications for pain, epilepsy and hearing, but those approaches remain at different stages of development. Some are still being tested in animals; any treatment would need to demonstrate safety as well as benefit.

content.headline: Apple’s new home range pairs a smart display with locks and cameras
content.shortHeadline: Apple unveils a smart-home display and new devices
content.standfirst: Apple is expanding its connected-home range around the $299 HomeView display, with a smart lock, doorbell, cameras and other devices also announced. The company’s new Siri features depend in part on an eligible iPhone and are not yet an independently tested alternative to rivals.

sources.originalTitle: Apple launches HomeView, its first smart display for the home
Apple’s HomeView display is now available to preorder
Apple’s new smart home lineup includes a smart lock, thermostat, and video doorbells

segments.body: The seven-inch HomeView is designed to control compatible smart-home devices, show recipes and camera feeds, and handle video calls. It costs $299, with preorders open and shipping due to start on 13 November. Apple says its Siri AI can answer natural-language requests and use personal context from messages, calendars and emails when an eligible iPhone is on the same network and the user is recognised.

segments.title: A broader home ecosystem
segments.body: Apple also announced a connected-home collection made with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, including a smart lock, doorbell, thermostat, temperature sensor and cameras. The lock is listed at $349.95 and the wired doorbell at $249.95; the devices are due in December. The Verge’s first-look report says the HomeView’s appeal will depend on how well its user recognition works and whether households want a shared screen tied closely to an iPhone.

content.headline: Bumble agrees to $1.3bn sale as dating app looks for a reset
content.shortHeadline: Bumble agrees to $1.3bn acquisition
content.standfirst: Ithaca Holdings has agreed to acquire Bumble, which would become privately owned after years of falling revenue and paying subscribers. Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd says she will remain involved as the company considers how to attract users.

sources.originalTitle: Bumble agrees to a $1.3B acquisition deal as online dating faces a reset
Dating app Bumble bought for $1.3bn

segments.body: Bumble has agreed to a $1.3bn acquisition by Ithaca Holdings. The transaction would take the dating-app company private. Co-founder Whitney Wolfe Herd plans to stay actively involved, working with Ithaca executives Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, according to the reports.

segments.title: Pressure to change the product
segments.body: Bumble’s revenue fell 15.2% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and its paying user base fell 16.4% to about 3.2 million, TechCrunch reports. The company has been exploring AI features and in-person activities, while Wolfe Herd has said it is developing ways to move beyond the familiar swipe-based model. The reports describe a proposed transaction; they do not establish what changes the new owner will make.

content.headline: Cyber incidents disrupt retailers in Britain and France
content.shortHeadline: Separate cyber incidents hit retailers
content.standfirst: A UK fashion group is investigating an incident affecting some systems, while a separate attack reportedly disabled connected refrigerators at French supermarkets and spoiled food. There is no evidence in the reports that the incidents are linked.

sources.originalTitle: Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim
French supermarket director apologises after cyber-attack spoils fresh and frozen food - video

segments.body: TFG London, the UK arm of South African retailer The Foschini Group, says a cybersecurity incident affected some IT systems and its Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles brands. It says stores remain open, although some website features may be unavailable, and that it is working with external specialists to investigate. The company said it did not believe payment information was affected, but was still checking whether other customer data was involved.

segments.title: A different kind of disruption
segments.body: Separately, French prosecutors said a large-scale attack was affecting connected refrigerators at several major food retailers. At one Intermarché store, the director said fridge temperatures reached 27C and fresh and frozen food was lost; the Guardian reported temperatures reaching as high as 50C at some supermarkets. The reports do not establish that the events share a perpetrator or cause.

content.headline: Thermal drones help find Cairngorms wildfire hotspots months later
content.shortHeadline: Drones find hotspots still burning beneath Cairngorms
content.standfirst: Thermal drone flights have located heat and smoke beneath the ground three months after a major Cairngorms wildfire. The images help crews target remaining hotspots, while the longer-term ecological effects are still unknown.

image.caption: Drone pilot Pete Short searches for wildfire hotspots in the Cairngorms.

sources.originalTitle: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms

segments.body: A wildfire that burned about 3,300 hectares in July has left hotspots smouldering under the soil. Drone pilot Pete Short uses thermal imaging to locate heat invisible from the surface, then sends the coordinates to land managers, who dispatch teams to dig and extinguish the remaining fire.

segments.title: Tracking recovery
segments.body: The same drone routes are being programmed to capture repeat images of the damaged landscape over time. Cairngorms National Park Authority conservation lead Sarah Henshall says it is too early to know the full ecological impact; recovery could take years or decades. The remaining hotspots also retain the potential to reignite a larger fire.

content.headline: Research links problematic social media use with health risks for young people
content.shortHeadline: Study links problematic media use to youth health risks
content.standfirst: A series of Lancet papers finds associations between problematic digital-media use and poorer mental health, sleep and physical activity among under-25s. Researchers say the links are modest and not conclusive, but call for more scrutiny and platform data.

sources.originalTitle: Three ways social media is harming young people, according to landmark study

segments.body: The three-paper series includes an analysis of reviews covering nine million people under 25. It links problematic digital-media use with higher risks of mental-health problems, sleep issues and reduced exercise. Researchers describe the associations as modest and do not establish that screen time alone causes those outcomes.

segments.title: Calls for scrutiny
segments.body: The researchers argue that platform design—including infinite scroll, autoplay and personalised recommendation feeds—deserves attention, and call on companies to share data for independent research. The series chair says the evidence warrants coordinated action; the papers do not settle which platform features cause harm or what measures would be most effective.

content.headline: Geoffrey Hinton argues uncertainty about AI risks is no reason for complacency
content.shortHeadline: Hinton says uncertainty is no reason to dismiss AI risks
content.standfirst: The AI pioneer argues that the possibility of systems escaping human control deserves serious attention, even though forecasts are uncertain. Nvidia chief Jensen Huang disputes the basis for some extinction estimates.

sources.originalTitle: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’

segments.body: Geoffrey Hinton says the point of putting a number on a low-probability catastrophe is to show that it merits attention, not to claim a precise forecast. He argues that increasingly capable AI systems could become difficult to control and that society should not dismiss that possibility simply because it is uncertain.

segments.title: Disagreement over the evidence
segments.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has called Hinton’s estimates of a 10–20% chance of AI-driven human extinction in coming decades unsupported by research and said such predictions can cause harm. Hinton responds that he is warning of a serious possibility rather than making a confident prediction. The interview also records Hinton’s views on AI understanding and consciousness; those are his interpretations, not established findings.

content.headline: Epic reportedly tells developers to use AI for a delayed Disney game
content.shortHeadline: Epic turns to AI for Disney game development
content.standfirst: Reports say developers on an unannounced Marvel and Star Wars game were told to use AI for code and artwork. Epic’s chief says the shift is meant to help teams make more, while a game designer warns that fully generated art could threaten creative work.

sources.originalTitle: Epic shifts to ‘AI-accelerated development’ for upcoming Disney game
Fortnite-maker Epic Games confirms 'huge pivot' towards using AI

segments.body: Epic Games has directed developers working on an unannounced Disney collaboration to use AI tools including Anthropic’s Claude, according to Bloomberg reporting cited by The Verge and the BBC. Staff were reportedly told there would be “no more hand-written code” and that artwork would be generated through AI workflows. The game, described as a shooter featuring Marvel and Star Wars characters, has been delayed from its original March release window.

segments.title: A disputed shift
segments.body: Epic CEO Tim Sweeney says AI is intended to help developers build more and better work, not simply to do the same work with fewer people. The BBC also spoke with game designer Lisha Howen, who accepts that developers may use AI to help with code but objects to fully AI-generated art, which she says can displace artists. Epic laid off more than 1,000 staff six months ago; Sweeney attributed those cuts to falling Fortnite engagement, not AI.

perspectives.body: Game designer Lisha Howen is not opposed to every use of AI, but says fully generated artwork can look poor and put artists’ jobs at risk.

content.headline: Character.AI files for bankruptcy as Disney offers to buy selected assets
content.shortHeadline: Character.AI files for bankruptcy; Disney is lead bidder
content.standfirst: The chatbot company has sought Chapter 11 protection and is offering selected assets to Disney for $20m. No final buyer has been secured, and Character.AI says its service could be shut down if the sale process fails.

sources.originalTitle: Character.AI files for bankruptcy
Just 5 years in, interactive chatbot platform Character.AI files for bankruptcy

segments.body: Character.AI has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US. Disney is the lead bidder for some of its assets, offering $20m and transition support, but the filing process is still under way. Character.AI lists estimated liabilities of $50m to $100m; the company says it will continue operating during the sale process, expected to conclude in late November or early December.

segments.title: Safety scrutiny and the platform’s future
segments.body: The company has faced lawsuits and scrutiny over chatbot safety, including a case brought after the suicide of a 14-year-old whose mother said he became obsessed with a bot. Character.AI has added safety features and banned minors from its platform. It says the service will be wound down if a suitable bid does not emerge; Disney’s proposed purchase of selected assets is not, by itself, a confirmed acquisition of the whole company.

content.headline: Meta releases new Muse models, citing its own benchmark results
content.shortHeadline: Meta launches Muse models, with performance claims unverified
content.standfirst: Meta says Muse Wonder and Wonder Full match leading models on selected benchmarks and will power its Muse agent. The company has not provided independent comparisons across the field, and says the models’ rollout will be limited at first.

sources.originalTitle: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
Meta has some Wonder Full new AI models

segments.body: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, its first models described as frontier systems. Wonder is available through Meta’s model API, while Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code subscribers. The company says both models will help power its Muse agent, but has not given a timeline for a wider release.

segments.title: Claims based on company testing
segments.body: Meta says its internal benchmark results put the models in range of systems from OpenAI and Anthropic, and highlights Wonder’s performance on a memory benchmark. The Verge notes that their standing against Google’s model remains unclear. Meta also set API prices for Wonder at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens; the reported comparisons are company claims, not independent evaluations.

perspectives.body: The Verge stresses that Meta’s comparisons rely on internal testing and that it is not yet clear how the new models compare with Google’s latest system.

content.headline: Amex proposes a framework to check AI agents’ purchases against user intent
content.shortHeadline: Amex proposes checks on AI-agent purchases
content.standfirst: American Express wants an industry framework to capture and authenticate what customers authorise AI agents to buy. The proposal is intended to prevent mistakes, but it has not yet become an industry standard and the company says it has not seen a rise in related disputes.

sources.originalTitle: Amex introduces a framework to prevent AI agents from making unauthorized purchases

segments.body: American Express’s proposed Intent Intelligence Framework would record a customer’s instructions and constraints, such as a preferred merchant or maximum price, before an AI agent completes a purchase. After the customer authenticates and approves those instructions, the system would create a token representing the authorised intent for use in the transaction.

segments.title: A proposal, not an established safeguard
segments.body: Amex says the approach could block a purchase if an agent strays from a customer’s request, and could help resolve disputes by recording what was authorised and when. The company says it has not yet seen an increase in disputes caused by agentic shopping; the framework is its proposal, and it hopes other businesses will adopt it. A survey cited by Amex found many US respondents were interested in using agents to research prices or recommendations.

content.headline: AFL tells Sportsbet to stop using players in AI-generated gambling videos
content.shortHeadline: AFL objects to AI videos using players without consent
content.standfirst: Sportsbet removed AI-generated videos depicting AFL players after the league and players’ association objected to their use in gambling promotion. The agreement governing image rights does not specifically address AI-generated material.

image.caption: A composite of AI-generated depictions of AFL players used by Sportsbet.

sources.originalTitle: AFL tells Sportsbet to stop using players in AI generated content

segments.body: The AFL told Sportsbet, its official gambling partner, to stop using prominent players in AI-generated social-media content without their permission. The videos depicted players Lachie Neale and Will Ashcroft delivering lines from speeches and television, and were removed after the Guardian contacted the company.

segments.title: Rules lag behind the technology
segments.body: The AFL Players’ Association said AI-generated player imagery was not permitted without approval and argued that the videos breached the league’s collective bargaining agreement with players. The agreement limits how partners may use player images but does not mention AI.
